p.span: Residential Tenancies Amendment (Rent Control) Bill 2026
First Reading
Bill introduced on motion by Ms Jenny Leong, read a first time and printed.
Second Reading Speech
Ms JENNY LEONG ( Newtown ) ( 10:18 :08 ): I move:
That this bill be now read a second time.

The rent is too damn high in New South Wales and it is getting worse. That is why I introduce the Residential Tenancies Amendment (Rent Control) Bill 2026. I do so as The Greens New South Wales spokesperson on housing and homelessness and as The Greens member for Newtown, where about 60 per cent of people rent. I acknowledge the renters and supporters of rent controls in the public gallery and watching online, including Patricia, who played a key role in getting this bill to where it is today.

I also acknowledge the tenant advocates and the CEO of the Tenants' Union of New South Wales, Leo Patterson Ross, who I believe will be watching online from their conference in Newcastle today. I acknowledge the powerful work of Everybody's Home, led by Maiy Azize; Shelter NSW; Homelessness NSW; the NSW Council of Social Service; and other housing and frontline services that recognise the growing need for the Government to regulate rents urgently.

The stress on renters is unbearable. Without urgent action it will only get worse. It is impossible to ignore the desperation that many in our communities feel as rents continue to rise, pushing them further into housing stress, poverty and even into homelessness. The hollow phrase "the cost-of-living crisis", uttered by those who pretend to care while choosing to do absolutely nothing about ever-increasing rents, makes me sick to my stomach. There is no greater way for this Parliament to release the pressure valve on our community and deliver much‑needed rent relief to millions who struggle every month with the cost of everything, including rents going up faster than wages, than to back the bill before the House to deliver rent controls for the people of New South Wales.

The reform will not cost the Government a single cent. There is no budget block to delivering this reform, yet the benefit to the daily budgets of everyone in this State will be real and felt immediately. Life feels hard. It feels stressful and it is challenging for many people right now. The pressure on anyone renting or anyone who loves someone who is renting is staggering. Sadly, it keeps getting worse. Across Sydney, 45 per cent of private renters live in rental stress, spending more than 30 per cent of their income on rent. Western Sydney has seen rental stress rates higher than 50 per cent. Since Labor was elected to government just three and a bit years ago, median rents in New South Wales have spiked 22 per cent. Imagine wages going up 22 per cent in that time. But no, just the rents have spiked.

The NSW Council of Social Service reports that almost one million people live in poverty, including one in seven children in this State. More than half are in extreme housing stress, spending more than half of their income on rent, up by one‑third since the Minns Government was elected. Those figures are terrifying. They demand an urgent solution. That solution is simple and is before us today. The Greens have done the work to solve the problem by introducing rent controls. Putting a freeze and cap on rents tackles the biggest expense facing one in three households in New South Wales, because rent rises are rapidly outpacing wages year on year.

Rent controls have been proven to be effective. They cost nothing to deliver and have a majority of public support across renters, mortgage holders and outright home owners. The top one per cent who conveniently own a quarter of all property investments wonder why we want to do this. Why do we allow them to unleash unlimited rent increases and extreme stress on half a million renters living in poverty just so they can expand their property empires? That wealth inequality, that generational inequity, that grotesque idea that people living in poverty can go hungry and skip medical appointments or basic essentials and work more and more hours just to keep shelter over their heads while their landlords collect more and more rent from them, is just sickening. Our system allows the one per cent to add millions to their children's trust funds, but by the age of 14 a kid living in rental accommodation will have moved more than six times, on average. That is a disgrace.

It does not stop there. With the financial pressure comes anxiety, stress, escalating mental health crises, social isolation from not being able to go out and have fun, and limits on being able to commute to work or class or travel the long distances that now exist between family, friends and support systems. Without rent controls, more and more people will retire into poverty after a lifetime of working or caring for their family. Without rent controls, essential workers will spend hours going to and from a job that barely pays the bills. Without rent controls, it will be much harder for victim-survivors to leave abusers.

Failing to act on out-of-control rents will further escalate the disadvantage and lack of dignity faced by people living with a disability, people who are unemployed or unable to work, and people who are currently languishing on the ever-growing public housing waiting list. For those at breaking point, there is currently no safety net, no backup and no protection, because the public and social housing waiting list has grown 25 per cent under the Labor Government. Unless we deliver rent controls for the private market, there is no escape from the brutal reality of not being able to afford the rent, or the stress of trying to find a way to scrape together the money to meet the next rent increase. All the while, we see mega-mansions bought up by uber wealthy people in our city, the massive profits of banks and property developers continue to rise, and governments fail to take urgent action to rein them in.

Why are we in this situation? For too long, laws passed in this Parliament have sided with investors and valued housing as a commodity rather than a human right. Shamefully, that is not surprising in light of recent parliamentary disclosures of how many politicians add to their already generous pay packets with passive income from rents. The Greens rent control bill before us today will change all of that. The bill will introduce a temporary freeze on rents for 12 months and then impose an ongoing permanent rent cap of 2 per cent on any rent increases tied to the property each year. It also gives renters a pathway to getting a rent reduction. A rent decrease is never heard of, despite the fact that we hear news of property prices dropping. The bill will also introduce a two-year fixed term lease as the standard, which is in line with the ask from the Australian Council of Trade Unions.

The Greens want to rein in profits of investors and developers. We make no apologies for that. We want to end the ever-rising price of houses and ever-increasing rents. We want to put an end to a system designed to always deliver more profits for developers and more return on investments for landlords. We have had enough. We regulate the cost of so many other essentials: child care, health care, transport and power bills. Even politicians' pay is regulated independently. Why not rents, the largest expense for millions of households? Why allow unlimited rent increases each year for millions of renters who are already under so much pressure? Why is the investor class given special privileges and protections while renters are denied their basic human rights to afford a decent, habitable place to call home?
When asked about the out-of-control costs of housing that are pushing tens of thousands of new applicants onto the social housing waiting list, the housing Minister said:

We don't have control over that, sadly. I don't have control over how much—cost-of-living pressures are increasing broadly in the economy. There are still significant pressures on the private rental market and private housing. These factors lead people to put their hands up for government housing.
But the Government and this Parliament do have control. Rents are the easiest part of the cost of housing for government to control, and it would not cost a single cent.

The bill that The Greens have brought before the Parliament today proves that there are very straightforward amendments that can happen to the Residential Tenancies Act that would introduce rent controls and relieve the unbearable pressures on millions of people. But up to this point the Premier, the housing Minister and this Labor Government have failed to act. Up to this point they have chosen to keep renters under intolerable stress. The Greens have done the work and brought a rent control bill to the Chamber and to the Parliament. Will the Government and the Opposition continue to wring their hands about the so‑called cost-of-living crisis, or will they step up, take responsibility, work with The Greens and pass this rent control bill before Christmas?

There is evidence from Australia and all over the world that rent controls work. Rent controls have been in place in the Australian Capital Territory since 2019, with rents capped at 110 per cent of the rent component of the consumer price index, which has supported much slower rent growth than other capital cities while having no impact on housing supply. A 2023 Macquarie University study looking at international examples and experiences of rent regulation prepared by the Tenants' Union NSW, Shelter NSW and researchers Dr Alistair Sisson—who I note is present in the gallery today—and Dr Penelope Bowyer-Pont found widespread evidence that rent regulation produces positive outcomes for tenants.

The study identified 25 OECD nations with forms of rent regulation, including Australia, 19 European nations, multiple states and cities across the United States and Canada, South Korea, Argentina and Brazil. It found a general consensus that rent regulation successfully reduces rents, moderates rent growth over time and improves security of tenure. It also found that where rent increases are made contingent on adequate repairs, and larger increases are made contingent on amenity improvements, rent controls improve housing quality across the jurisdiction. Further, it found scant evidence of rent regulation reducing construction activity, despite this claim being a common feature of the public debate. This is consistent with the seven years that we have seen that evidence play out in reality for the people of the Australian Capital Territory.
